header.title: why metabolic rate increases during exercise
header.subject: Biology

sequence.heading: Where this lesson sits
carried_forward: Last lesson covered: the structure and function of mitochondria.

content.text: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to analyse the link between increased ATP demand in muscles and the rise in oxygen consumption and heart rate during exercise.
content.note: Learners correctly sequence and label the rest-exercise-recovery diagram, showing the cause (ATP demand) leading to the effect (higher oxygen consumption/heart rate).

content.text: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to analyse why heart rate and breathing remain elevated after exercise stops, by explaining the connection to EPOC and continued oxygen use for ATP resynthesis.
content.note: In the group poster and short presentation, learners produce a correct cause-effect sentence for the recovery phase using the term EPOC and at least one supporting reason from the input.

language.text: Learners will use the words metabolic rate, ATP, resynthesize, oxidative phosphorylation, oxygen consumption, cardiorespiratory system, EPOC and heart rate to describe what happens to the body during and after exercise.
Learners will use cause-and-effect language (because, so, as a result, this happens because) to link a biological cause to its effect on heart rate or oxygen consumption.
While building their timeline poster, learners will notice and reuse phrases such as 'stays high' and 'returns to normal' that emerge naturally from comparing the three phases.

objectives.learning_skill: Learners will work with a partner or group and report a shared answer.

stages.name: Bridge back
stages.purpose: Make the link to prior learning explicit, so this lesson is felt as part of a sequence.
teacher_does: Show one image or object from the previous lesson and ask learners what they remember.
Record two or three remembered terms where everyone can see them.
Say in one sentence how today follows on.
learners_do: In pairs, recall two things from last time before anyone answers aloud.
Add one term to the shared list.
stages.language_focus: Recall and naming. Accept the first language here if it speeds up retrieval.
stages.watch_for: Do not let this become a full review lesson. It is a doorway, not a room.

stages.name: Pre-task scaffold
stages.purpose: Remove the language barrier before the content arrives, not during it.
teacher_does: Pre-teach no more than eight key Biology terms, each with a visual or a first-language gloss.
Display the sentence frames from the language bank and model one aloud.
Check understanding with a quick non-verbal response, such as pointing, holding up fingers or matching.
learners_do: Match terms to images with a partner, then compare with another pair.
Say one frame aloud once, so the first use is not during the task.
stages.language_focus: Language of learning. Up to 250 words of new text with a glossary.
stages.watch_for: If learners cannot use a frame here, they will not use it in the task. Slow down rather than continue.

stages.name: Content input
stages.purpose: Start by showing that contracting muscle needs a constant ATP supply but only stores a little, so it must be resynthesized fast during exercise [1]. Explain that this resynthesis mostly happens through oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria, which needs oxygen delivered by the cardiorespiratory system, so heart rate and breathing rise together with ATP demand [1,4]. Show that metabolic rate can rise to 5-15 times resting level during exercise [2]. Then introduce EPOC: after exercise stops, oxygen consumption and metabolic rate stay above resting level, with a main phase of about 2 hours and a smaller effect up to 48 hours, because the body is still resynthesizing ATP and restoring systems to rest [4,6].
teacher_does: Simple ATP-ADP cycle diagram with the word 'resynthesize'
Three-phase timeline sketch: REST - EXERCISE - RECOVERY (unlabelled, to be completed later)
Key vocabulary list with the 8 target terms
Short graph shape showing oxygen consumption rising then staying elevated after exercise stops
learners_do: Answer: Why does the body need more ATP during exercise? (expected: Because muscles are contracting more and ATP stores are small, so ATP must be resynthesized quickly [1].)
Answer: What does the cardiorespiratory system do during exercise? (expected: It delivers more oxygen to the muscles so oxidative phosphorylation can resynthesize ATP faster [1,4].)
Answer: What happens to oxygen consumption right after exercise stops? (expected: It stays higher than resting level for a while; this is called EPOC [4,6].)
stages.language_focus: Receptive. Learners need to understand, not yet to produce.
stages.watch_for: Long unbroken teacher talk is the most common failure point in CLIL input. Chunk it.

stages.name: Main task: EPOC Timeline Poster
stages.purpose: A shared online three-phase timeline diagram (rest, exercise, recovery) that each group labels and annotates with one cause-effect sentence per phase, explaining why heart rate and oxygen consumption change, especially why they stay high in recovery.
teacher_does: Model one completed phase (exercise) on screen, thinking aloud with a sentence frame.
Assign learners to breakout rooms of 3-4 with a shared slide/doc containing the blank three-phase timeline.
Circulate through breakout rooms to prompt with checking questions and vocabulary reminders.
Bring groups back and have each group share their recovery-phase sentence on screen.
Ask the class to compare sentences and agree on the best explanation of EPOC as a whole class.
learners_do: In your group, look at the blank timeline: rest, exercise, recovery.
For each phase, decide what happens to heart rate and oxygen consumption.
Write one sentence per phase using a frame from the language bank and at least one vocabulary term.
Agree as a group on your best sentence for the recovery phase, using the word EPOC.
Choose one member to present your recovery sentence to the class.
stages.language_focus: Learners must write and justify cause-effect sentences using the target vocabulary and frames, so the reasoning cannot be shown through drawing alone.
stages.watch_for: If groups fall silent, the language support is missing, not the motivation.
differentiation: Less confident: Give a partly completed timeline with the rest and exercise sentences already modelled, so the group only needs to complete the recovery phase using the frame and word bank.
More confident: Ask these groups to add a second sentence linking their recovery explanation to oxidative phosphorylation or ATP resynthesis, without using the frame.
Mixed group: Pair a more confident learner with less confident peers in each breakout room and assign the confident learner as 'vocabulary checker' before the group finalises its sentence.

stages.name: Report and check
stages.purpose: Make learning visible, and gather evidence against both objectives separately.
teacher_does: Take one report per group, holding others to listening with a specific question.
Give one piece of content feedback and one piece of language feedback, clearly labelled as such.
Record who met the content objective and who met the language objective. They are not the same list.
learners_do: Report the outcome using the frames.
Complete a one-question exit check on the content, answerable in the first language if needed.
stages.language_focus: Language through learning. Capture what emerged and reuse it next lesson.
stages.watch_for: Judging content understanding through language accuracy is the classic CLIL assessment error. Separate them.
evidence: Content evidence: the exit check and the correctness of the task outcome.
Language evidence: use of the target frames during the task and the report.

brief.claim: Muscle cells store only a small amount of ATP, so ATP must be continually resynthesized for muscle contraction to continue.
As exercise intensity increases, the rate at which ATP is used increases greatly, so the pathways that resynthesize ATP must work faster.
Oxidative phosphorylation resynthesizes ATP using oxygen that is delivered to the muscle by the respiratory and cardiovascular systems.
Muscular exercise can increase metabolism to 5 to 15 times the resting rate to supply energy for muscle contraction.
The harder the muscles work, the faster the heart beats, because this supports greater oxygen delivery to the working muscles.
ATP is generated by mitochondria through oxidative phosphorylation, a process that consumes oxygen.
Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) is a rise in metabolic rate above resting level that continues after exercise has stopped, typically for up to a few hours.
EPOC has two phases: one lasting about 2 hours, and a smaller, more prolonged effect that can last up to 48 hours.

misconceptions.learners_think: Heart rate and breathing return to normal the moment exercise stops.
misconceptions.why_it_is_wrong: Metabolic rate stays above its resting level for a period after exercise ends, so the body still needs extra oxygen.
misconceptions.what_is_correct: This continued elevation is called EPOC (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption) and can last from about 2 hours up to 48 hours.

misconceptions.learners_think: Lactate is only made without oxygen and it is what causes muscle fatigue.
misconceptions.why_it_is_wrong: Lactate is actually an important fuel that muscles can use for energy, not simply a waste product that causes tiredness.
misconceptions.what_is_correct: Lactate produced during contraction is an important energy-yielding substrate for the muscle.

misconceptions.learners_think: The body only starts using fat for energy once carbohydrate has run out.
misconceptions.why_it_is_wrong: Fat and carbohydrate are used together during exercise, with the balance depending on exercise intensity, not on carbohydrate running out first.
misconceptions.what_is_correct: At lower intensities lipid oxidation dominates, and reliance on carbohydrate increases as intensity rises.

gaps: The corpus does not explain the specific mechanism linking breathing rate (as opposed to heart rate) to recovery oxygen demand, so the lesson focuses mainly on heart rate and oxygen consumption for breathing-related claims.
No source provides a ready-made labelled diagram or graph image; the teacher will need to sketch the three-phase timeline based on the described data.
The corpus does not give age-specific classroom data (e.g. typical teenage heart rate values), so no numerical heart-rate figures for learners this age are included.

worksheet.title: Why Does Your Heart Keep Racing After You Stop Running?
worksheet.learner_instructions: Work through Parts 1-5 using the vocabulary and sentence frames in the box below. You can look back at the board notes and your group poster to help you.
language_help_box: Key words: metabolic rate, ATP, resynthesize, oxidative phosphorylation, oxygen consumption, cardiorespiratory system, EPOC, heart rate
Frame 1: Heart rate increases because the muscles need more ___.
Frame 2: During exercise, oxygen consumption rises because ATP must be ___.
Frame 3: After exercise stops, ___ stays high because the body is still repaying an oxygen ___.
Frame 4: This is called ___, and it can last for ___.
Connector words: because / so / as a result / this happens because

parts.heading: Explain EPOC
parts.instructions: In 2-3 sentences, explain why heart rate and oxygen consumption stay high after exercise stops. Use the word EPOC and at least one reason from the lesson.

items.prompt: Why do heart rate and oxygen consumption stay high after exercise stops?

exit_check.prompt: In one sentence (Spanish is fine), why does your breathing stay fast for a while after you stop running?
exit_check.note: Accept an answer in Spanish or English; the idea of continued oxygen use/EPOC is what matters, not perfect wording.

teacher_script: Look at this diagram: ATP turns into ADP and back again - this is what we call 'resynthesize'.
Muscles only store a little ATP, so during exercise this cycle must happen very fast - that's why oxygen consumption rises so quickly.
Watch this graph: oxygen consumption goes up during exercise... but look what happens right after exercise stops - it doesn't drop straight away.
This staying-high effect is called EPOC - excess post-exercise oxygen consumption - and it can last up to 48 hours.
In your breakout groups, complete the timeline poster: write one sentence for each phase using the frames on your worksheet.
Let's compare your recovery-phase sentences - which one best explains why oxygen consumption stays high?

checks.name: Every subject claim traces to a source
checks.note: All 8 subject_brief items map to a cited source and the wording is a faithful paraphrase (e.g. 5-15x metabolic rate from Source 2, EPOC phase lengths from Source 6). Claim 5 (Fick's principle/heart rate) is a slightly loose paraphrase of Source 4 but still faithful to intent.

checks.name: No fact contradicts the corpus
checks.note: No statement in subject_brief, vocabulary, or worksheet directly contradicts a corpus-stated fact. The 'oxygen debt' framing (see outdated-science check) is not sourced but also isn't a direct contradiction of anything the corpus states.

checks.name: No outdated or disputed science presented as settled
checks.note: Language Bank Frame 3 and its answer key ('the body is still repaying an oxygen debt') presents the classical 'oxygen debt' model as the correct answer. This model is considered an oversimplification/outdated in current exercise physiology (EPOC is now attributed to multiple factors: ATP/PCr resynthesis, elevated body temperature, catecholamines, lactate clearance - not a simple 'debt' being 'repaid'). It is not supported by any of the six sources and should be removed or reframed.

checks.name: Objectives achievable in the lesson length
checks.note: 50 minutes online must cover input stage, vocabulary, breakout-room poster task with circulation, whole-class share-back, AND a 5-part worksheet plus exit check. This is ambitious; teacher should confirm real timings, especially breakout room set-up/return overhead typical of online group classes.

checks.name: Cognitive demand matches the stated Bloom level
checks.note: The main task (timeline poster, cause-effect sentences) and Worksheet Parts 2 and 5 genuinely reach Analyse. However, Part 1 (matching) and Part 3 (gap-fill) are Remember/Understand level. This scaffolding is defensible for A2-B1 learners but the teacher should confirm the lesson still culminates in genuine analysis for all groups, not just the strongest ones.

checks.name: Vocabulary load within the cap
checks.note: Exactly 8 new terms listed, matching the stated cap.

checks.name: Language on the worksheet matches the support level
checks.note: Several model/answer sentences (e.g. 'the body is still resynthesizing ATP and restoring the muscles and cardiorespiratory system to rest') and terms like 'oxidative phosphorylation', 'cardiorespiratory system' are dense for A2-B1. The frames themselves are manageable, but the extended-response and answer-key language likely exceeds what learners can produce unsupported; teacher should confirm scaffolding (sentence starters, L1 support) is sufficient in practice.

checks.name: Task genuinely requires the target language
checks.note: The poster task requires learners to produce cause-effect sentences in English using target vocabulary; content cannot be conveyed by labels/drawing alone.

checks.name: Task outcome is concrete, not a verb list
checks.note: Outcome is a specific artefact (shared three-phase timeline poster with one annotated sentence per phase) and a short presentation, not just a list of Bloom verbs.

checks.name: Every worksheet item has an answer
checks.note: All items in Parts 1-5 have a corresponding answer_key entry with matching count. The exit_check has embedded guidance rather than a formal answer_key entry, but this is appropriate for an open, formative, L1-permitted check.

checks.name: Content and language assessed separately
checks.note: Each worksheet part is explicitly tagged 'language' or 'content' in the 'assesses' field, and this split is consistent with the stated content/language objectives.

checks.name: Age and register appropriate for the learner group
checks.note: Topic framing ('Why Does Your Heart Keep Racing After You Stop Running?'), examples, and allowance for L1 in the exit check are appropriate for 14-18 year olds; register is neutral and non-patronising.

unsupported_claims.claim: 'After exercise stops, [X] stays high because the body is still repaying an oxygen debt' (Language Bank Frame 3 and its answer key entry: 'oxygen debt').
unsupported_claims.why: The 'oxygen debt' concept is not present in any of the six corpus sources and reflects an outdated/oversimplified model of EPOC. Sources 4 and 6 describe EPOC in terms of continued ATP resynthesis and multi-hour elevation of metabolic rate, not a 'debt' being 'repaid'. Presenting this as the expected correct answer risks teaching a discredited mechanism as settled fact.

teacher_must_confirm: Whether the 50-minute online slot realistically allows for input + breakout-room poster work + return/share-back + all 5 worksheet parts + exit check, or whether Parts 3-4 should be set as homework.

Whether to remove or replace the 'oxygen debt' phrasing in the Language Bank frame and answer key with a phrasing grounded in the supplied sources (e.g. 'the body is still using extra oxygen to resynthesise ATP').

Whether learners at A2-B1 can realistically produce the extended-response sentences modelled in the answer key unassisted, or whether more sentence scaffolding is needed in the online breakout format.
Whether breakout-room technology and shared docs/slides are confirmed working for this specific group before the lesson, given the task depends entirely on this online group mechanic.

Whether Part 4's 'rewrite the false sentence correctly' task is too demanding a free-writing task for the weakest learners in this A2-B1 range, and whether a rewritten multiple-choice correction format is preferable.

generation.note: Subject content written from 6 retrieved sources and audited by a second pass. Claims carry source numbers. Anything the audit could not confirm is flagged rather than hidden.
